1 Purpose of this session

This file describes the different steps to perform the enrichment part of the single cell RNAseq data analysis training course for the EB3I n1 2026, covering these steps :

  • Load a gene set from different sources
  • Perform enrichment analysis
  • Plot results

Input data: A result of differential expression analysis

Output data: A list of gene set enriched

A lot of different packages exist but a lot of them are different embedding of the same algorithms. Here, you will discover clusterProfiler, a widely used R package to perform enrichment analyses.

2 Start RStudio

Using the OpenOnDemand/Rstudio cheat sheet, connect to the OpenOnDemand portal and create a Rstudio session with the right resource requirements, thanks to the cheat sheet.

4 Load gene set

QUESTION

What is a gene set?

ANSWER

It is a list of genes linked to a biological insight like a function, a transcription factor, a cell type…

There are multiple ways for loading them.

The R package ClusterProfiler is installed with other packages (i.e. dependencies) that allow to retrieve databases either from web or directly from packages. We take the example of Gene Ontology database.

# Show already loaded Gene Ontology database

Warning

Loading databases from R or the internet is an obstacle to reproducibility :

  • updating R packages changes database contents
  • databases on the internet are updated frequently

Enrichment analyses are highly sensitive to database changes.

4.3 From file

This file can come from a loaded database or can be homemade by taking gene lists from publications. The usual format is GMT : a tabulated text file with the first column as the name of the gene list, the second column as a description of this gene list and as many columns as the number of genes in this gene list. So each row has a different number of columns.

You can also work from a classic table like the one printed below.

Code 
load_geneset_file
# Loads the data from a file stored
go_from_file <- read.gmt("m5.go.bp.v2026.1.Mm.symbols.gmt")

# Prints the beginning of a table
knitr::kable(head(go_from_file))

QUESTION

Is the size number of a gene set important and why?

ANSWER

Yes it is important because gene sets with a low number of genes (below 10-20) decrease the performance of enrichment analyses. On the other hand, a gene set with too many genes (above 2000-5000) corresponds to a too generic function.

clusterProfiler uses minGSSize and maxGSSize parameters to select only gene set in a certain range of size.

Code 
markers_list <- FindAllMarkers(object = scdata, only.pos = FALSE, 
                               min.pct = 0.25, 
                               thresh.use = 0)

  • Over Representation Analyses (ORA)
  • Gene Set Enrichment Analyses (GSEA)

4.4 Prepare your list of genes

You already have your gene set. You now need to extract genes from your differential expression analyses.

QUESTION

What kind of input gene list is needed to run ORA?

ANSWER

Any list of genes. Be carreful to use the same gene identifiers as what is used for the gene set.

QUESTION

What metric(s) could be used to generate a list of genes?

ANSWER
  • adjusted p-value to select significative DEGs
  • average log2FC to select genes that are highly differential between the compared samples

4.5 Perform

The Over Representation Analyses can be performed with the enricher() function of clusterProfiler.

Code 
compare_ora
# Filter markers

#     ungroup()

# ora_compare_clusters <- compareCluster(gene ~ cluster, data = list_ora, fun = 'enricher', TERM2GENE = go_from_file)
# 
# dotplot(ora_compare_clusters, label_format = 40) + 
#     theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
Code 
compare_gsea
# list_gsea <- markers_list |> 
#     arrange(desc(avg_log2FC))
# 
# gsea_compare_clusters <- compareCluster(gene | avg_log2FC ~ cluster, data = list_gsea, fun = 'GSEA', TERM2GENE = go_from_file)
# 
# dotplot(gsea_compare_clusters, font.size=8, showCategory=5, title =("GSEA Hallmark database"), split=".sign") + facet_grid(.~.sign)

QUESTION

What are the three inputs required to perform enrichment analyses?

ANSWER
  1. Omics data : expression or statistics
  2. A reference database: list of genes linked to a specific function
  3. A statistic method to perform the enrichment
QUESTION

What are the differences between ORA, GSEA and AUCell?

ANSWER
  • ORA performs a fisher exact test on a non weighted list of genes selected using an arbitrary cut-off.
  • GSEA performs a weighted Kolmogorov-Smirnov test on a gene list ordered by log2FC.
  • AUCell calculates a score based on the proportion of genes from a gene set in the highly expressed genes for each cell.

# Purpose of this session {#purpose-of-this-session}

This file describes the different steps to perform the **enrichment part** of the **single cell RNAseq** data analysis training course for the **EB3I n1 2026**, covering these steps :

-   **Load** a **gene set** from different sources
-   **Perform** enrichment analysis
-   **Plot** results

**Input data**: A result of differential expression analysis

**Output data**: A list of gene set enriched

A lot of different packages exist but a lot of them are different embedding of the same algorithms. Here, you will discover clusterProfiler, a widely used R package to perform enrichment analyses.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Start RStudio

Using the [OpenOnDemand/Rstudio cheat sheet](https://moodle.france-bioinformatique.fr/pluginfile.php/1475/mod_folder/content/0/OoD_R_Rstudio.html), connect to the [OpenOnDemand portal](https://ondemand.cluster.france-bioinformatique.fr/) and create a Rstudio session with the right resource requirements, thanks to the cheat sheet.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Environment

## Set parameters

We now set common parameters as new variables, once and for all for this session :

::: callout-warning
**DO NOT** just run this with `ebaii_sc_teachers` project name as-is, put **YOURS** !
:::

```{r}
#| label: fs_set_pjname
#| filename: fs_set_pjname

## Set your project name
project_name <- "ebaii_sc_teachers" # <1>

## Control if the project_name exists on the cluster
cat('PATH CHECK : ', dir.exists(paste0('/shared/projects/', project_name))) # <2>

## Seed for the GSEA
my_seed <- 42 # <3>
```

1.  Uncomment this line and specify YOUR project name
2.  Should return "PATH CHECK : TRUE" if project_name exists
3.  You can choose another value before running analysis but if you change it, you'll get different results

## Load all needed libraries

We load the packages we will need for the analysis.

```{r, message=FALSE}
#| label: load_environment 
#| filename: load_environment  

## TODO : libraries to load
library(Seurat) # <1>
library(clusterProfiler, quietly = TRUE) # <2> 
library(org.Mm.eg.db, quietly = TRUE) # <3>
library(dplyr, quietly = TRUE) # <4>
library(ggplot2, quietly = TRUE)  # <5>
```

1.  For scRNAseq analyses
2.  Perform enrichment analysis [@yuBiomedicalKnowledgeMining2025]
3.  Mouse genes with identifier correspondences. If human, you can specify org.Hs.eg.db.
4.  Perform table modifications
5.  Perform graphics

# Load gene set {#sec-geneset}

::: {.callout-note icon="false" style="background: lightblue"}
## QUESTION

What is a gene set?
:::

::: {.callout-note icon="false" collapse="true" style="background: lightgreen"}
## ANSWER

It is a list of genes linked to a biological insight like a function, a transcription factor, a cell type...
:::

There are multiple ways for loading them.

The R package ClusterProfiler is installed with other packages (i.e. dependencies) that allow to retrieve databases either from web or directly from packages. We take the example of [Gene Ontology database](https://geneontology.org/docs/ontology-documentation/).

## From R packages

```{r}
#| label: load_geneset_r
#| filename: load_geneset_r

# Show already loaded Gene Ontology database
GO.db::GO_dbInfo()
```

## From the Web
```{r}
# Load the MSigDB database for the mouse organism
# If db_species not specified, it loads the human database with the mouse ortholog genes
go_from_web <- msigdbr::msigdbr(species = 'mouse', collection = "M5", subcollection = "GO:BP", db_species = 'MM')

# Prints the beginning of the table
knitr::kable(head(go_from_web))

# Prints the list of gene ontologies in the database
knitr::kable(head(table(go_from_web$gs_name), 5), col.names = c("term", "nb of genes"))
```

::: callout-important
## Warning

Loading databases from **R** or the **internet** is an **obstacle to reproducibility** :

-   updating R packages changes database contents
-   databases on the internet are updated frequently

Enrichment analyses are **highly sensitive** to database changes.
:::

## From file

This file can come from a loaded database or can be homemade by taking gene lists from publications. The usual format is [GMT](https://docs.gsea-msigdb.org/#GSEA/Data_Formats/#gmt-gene-matrix-transposed-file-format-gmt) : a tabulated text file with the first column as the name of the gene list, the second column as a description of this gene list and as many columns as the number of genes in this gene list. So each row has a different number of columns.

You can also work from a classic table like the one printed below.

```{r}
#| label: load_geneset_file
#| filename: load_geneset_file

# Loads the data from a file stored
go_from_file <- read.gmt("m5.go.bp.v2026.1.Mm.symbols.gmt")

# Prints the beginning of a table
knitr::kable(head(go_from_file))

# Prints some terms and the number of genes that compose those terms
knitr::kable(head(table(go_from_file$term), 5), col.names = c("term", "nb of genes"))
```

::: {.callout-note icon="false" style="background: lightblue"}
## QUESTION

Is the size number of a gene set important and why?
:::

::: {.callout-note icon="false" collapse="true" style="background: lightgreen"}
## ANSWER

Yes it is important because gene sets with a low number of genes (below 10-20) decrease the performance of enrichment analyses. On the other hand, a gene set with too many genes (above 2000-5000) corresponds to a too generic function.

clusterProfiler uses minGSSize and maxGSSize parameters to select only gene set in a certain range of size.
:::

```{r}
markers_list <- FindAllMarkers(object = scdata, only.pos = FALSE, 
                               min.pct = 0.25, 
                               thresh.use = 0)
```

# Over Representation Analyses (ORA)

## Prepare your list of genes

You already have your gene set. You now need to extract genes from your differential expression analyses.

::: {.callout-note icon="false" style="background: lightblue"}
## QUESTION

What kind of input gene list is needed to run ORA?
:::

::: {.callout-note icon="false" collapse="true" style="background: lightgreen"}
## ANSWER

Any list of genes. Be carreful to use the same gene identifiers as what is used for the gene set.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon="false" style="background: lightblue"}
## QUESTION

What metric(s) could be used to generate a list of genes?
:::

::: {.callout-note icon="false" collapse="true" style="background: lightgreen"}
## ANSWER

- adjusted p-value to select significative DEGs
- average log2FC to select genes that are highly differential between the compared samples
:::

## Perform 

The Over Representation Analyses can be performed with the `enricher()` function of clusterProfiler.

```{r}
#| label: compare_ora
#| filename: compare_ora

# Filter markers
# list_ora <- markers_list |> 
#     group_by(cluster) |> 
#     filter(p_val_adj < 0.01) |> 
#     ungroup()
# 
# ora_compare_clusters <- compareCluster(gene ~ cluster, data = list_ora, fun = 'enricher', TERM2GENE = go_from_file)
# 
# dotplot(ora_compare_clusters, label_format = 40) + 
#     theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

# Gene Set Enrichment Analyses (GSEA)

```{r}
#| label: compare_gsea
#| filename: compare_gsea
# list_gsea <- markers_list |> 
#     arrange(desc(avg_log2FC))
# 
# gsea_compare_clusters <- compareCluster(gene | avg_log2FC ~ cluster, data = list_gsea, fun = 'GSEA', TERM2GENE = go_from_file)

# dotplot(gsea_compare_clusters, font.size=8, showCategory=5, title =("GSEA Hallmark database"), split=".sign") + facet_grid(.~.sign)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

::: {.callout-note icon="false" style="background: lightblue"}
## QUESTION

What are the three inputs required to perform enrichment analyses?
:::

::: {.callout-note icon="false" collapse="true" style="background: lightgreen"}
## ANSWER

1.  Omics data : expression or statistics
2.  A reference database: list of genes linked to a specific function
3.  A statistic method to perform the enrichment
:::

::: {.callout-note icon="false" style="background: lightblue"}
## QUESTION

What are the differences between ORA, GSEA and AUCell?
:::

::: {.callout-note icon="false" collapse="true" style="background: lightgreen"}
## ANSWER

-   **ORA** performs a fisher exact test on a non weighted list of genes selected using an arbitrary cut-off.
-   **GSEA** performs a weighted Kolmogorov-Smirnov test on a gene list ordered by log2FC.
-   **AUCell** calculates a score based on the proportion of genes from a gene set in the highly expressed genes for each cell.
:::
